title: Top-N per group with RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY) — how do you get top 2 per department without collapsing rows?
description: Use window RANK() to rank within partitions and filter the ranked CTE; compare with GROUP BY limits.
answer:
`RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY score DESC)` numbers rows *within each partition* without collapsing them; wrap in a CTE and filter `WHERE rnk <= N` for top-N per group. Ties share a rank and leave gaps — use `DENSE_RANK` or `ROW_NUMBER` when gaps matter.
| Function | Ties | Gap after tie | Use when | |---|---|---|---| | `ROW_NUMBER()` | unique 1,2,3 | no tie concept | Need exactly N rows, dedup | | `RANK()` | same rank | **yes** (1,1,3) | Olympic ranking, allow more than N on ties | | `DENSE_RANK()` | same rank | **no** (1,1,2) | Tier/level assignment | > **Tip:** For strict “exactly 2 per dept” use `ROW_NUMBER()`. For “top 2 distinct scores including ties” use `DENSE_RANK() <= 2`. Add a deterministic tiebreaker `ORDER BY score DESC, id ASC` so repeated runs are stable. ```sql -- Top 2 earners per department (ties share rank; may return 3 if 2nd place ties) WITH ranked AS ( SELECT id, dept, name, salary, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC, id) AS rn FROM employees ) SELECT id, dept, name, salary, rnk FROM ranked WHERE rnk <= 2 -- use rn <= 2 for exactly 2 rows per dept ORDER BY dept, rnk, id; -- Alternative: DENSE_RANK for top 2 distinct salary levels SELECT * FROM ( SELECT *, DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) AS dr FROM employees ) t WHERE dr <= 2; ```

title: RANK() vs DENSE_RANK() vs ROW_NUMBER() — when does the gap matter and how do you choose?
description: Deep dive into ranking semantics, partition ordering, and performance implications for leaderboards.
answer:
All three enumerate within a window, but only `RANK` leaves gaps after ties (`1,1,3`), `DENSE_RANK` doesn’t (`1,1,2`), and `ROW_NUMBER` never ties. Pick by whether you count *rows* or *distinct values*.
| Scenario | Correct function | Why | |---|---|---| | Leaderboard top-10 distinct scores | `DENSE_RANK() <= 10` | 10 tiers, not 10 people | | Paginated winners (exactly 10) | `ROW_NUMBER() <= 10` | Deterministic count | | Olympic medals (shared silver skips bronze) | `RANK()` | Gap reflects skipped position | | Dedup keep latest per key | `ROW_NUMBER() … ORDER BY updated_at DESC` + `rn=1` | One survivor per partition | > **Tip:** Without `ORDER BY` inside `OVER()` the rank is nondeterministic. Always add a tiebreaker (`id` or `created_at`) and consider `NULLS LAST` — `ORDER BY score DESC NULLS LAST` — so NULLs don’t steal rank 1. ```sql -- Leaderboard: rank, dense_rank, row_number side-by-side SELECT name, dept, score, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY score DESC, id) AS rn, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY score DESC) AS rnk, DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY score DESC) AS drnk FROM employees ORDER BY dept, score DESC; -- Keep only latest row per (user_id) — classic dedup pattern WITH dedup AS ( SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY updated_at DESC) AS rn FROM events ) SELECT * FROM dedup WHERE rn = 1; ```

title: Recursive CTE for an org chart — how do you list all reports (direct + indirect) of a manager?
description: Anchor + recursive term to traverse a manager → employee hierarchy and compute depth/path.
answer:
A recursive CTE has an *anchor* (base rows) `UNION ALL` a *recursive* term that joins the CTE back to the table. Start at the manager, repeatedly join `manager_id = cte.id`, and track `depth`/`path`.
| Clause part | Role | Gotcha | |---|---|---| | Anchor `SELECT … WHERE manager_id IS NULL` | Seed rows (CEO or chosen manager) | Must be non-recursive | | `UNION ALL` | Append next level each iteration | `UNION` (distinct) is slower + hides cycles | | Recursive `JOIN employees e ON e.manager_id = c.id` | Expand one level | Needs index on `manager_id` | | Termination | No new rows or `depth < 20` | Add depth guard to avoid runaway | > **Tip:** Create `CREATE INDEX ON employees(manager_id)` — without it each recursion does a seq scan. Use `UNION ALL` not `UNION`; dedup is wasteful when the hierarchy is a tree. ```sql -- All reports under manager 42 with depth and path WITH RECURSIVE org AS ( -- anchor: the manager themselves (depth 0) SELECT id, name, manager_id, 0 AS depth, ARRAY[id] AS path FROM employees WHERE id = 42 UNION ALL -- recursive: direct reports of anyone already in org SELECT e.id, e.name, e.manager_id, o.depth + 1, o.path || e.id FROM employees e JOIN org o ON e.manager_id = o.id WHERE o.depth < 20 -- safety guard ) SELECT id, name, depth, path FROM org ORDER BY depth, name; -- Whole company tree starting at CEO(s) -- anchor: WHERE manager_id IS NULL ```

title: Recursive CTE with cycle detection — how do you handle circular manager references and produce a search order?
description: Use path array or PG 14+ CYCLE / SEARCH clauses to prevent infinite recursion and order hierarchically.
answer:
Track a `path` array and filter `WHERE id <> ALL(path)` or use Postgres 14+ `CYCLE` + `SEARCH` clauses. `SEARCH BREADTH FIRST` gives level-order; `DEPTH FIRST` gives pre-order traversal.
| Technique | Syntax | When to use | |---|---|---| | Manual path array | `path || e.id` + `WHERE e.id <> ALL(path)` | Portable, works on any PG version | | `CYCLE` clause | `CYCLE id SET is_cycle USING path` | PG 14+, auto-detects any cycle, sets flag | | `SEARCH BREADTH FIRST` | `SEARCH BREADTH FIRST BY id SET ordercol` | Need deterministic level-order output | | Depth guard | `WHERE depth < 50` | Defense-in-depth, always add | > **Tip:** Even with `CYCLE`, keep `depth < N` — a cycle detector stops loops but a 10M-row hierarchy still needs a cutoff. For org charts, `BREADTH FIRST` is usually more readable than `DEPTH FIRST`. ```sql -- PG 14+ idiomatic: automatic cycle detection + breadth-first order WITH RECURSIVE org(id, name, manager_id, depth, path) AS ( SELECT id, name, manager_id, 0, ARRAY[id] FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NULL UNION ALL SELECT e.id, e.name, e.manager_id, o.depth + 1, o.path || e.id FROM employees e JOIN org o ON e.manager_id = o.id WHERE e.id <> ALL(o.path) -- manual guard (redundant with CYCLE but portable) ) SEARCH BREADTH FIRST BY id SET ordercol CYCLE id SET is_cycle USING path SELECT id, name, depth, is_cycle, ordercol FROM org ORDER BY ordercol; -- Pre-PG14 alternative is identical but without SEARCH/CYCLE keywords -- rely solely on path array + WHERE check above. ```

title: LATERAL JOIN — how do you fetch the top 3 orders per customer efficiently?
description: Use CROSS/LEFT JOIN LATERAL as a per-row correlated subquery that can return multiple columns without aggregation.
answer:
`JOIN LATERAL` (or `CROSS APPLY` in SQL Server) lets the right-hand subquery reference columns from the left row and runs once per outer row. Perfect for “top-N per group” with an index on `(customer_id, order_date DESC)`.
| Join type | Keeps customers with 0 orders? | Typical use | |---|---|---| | `CROSS JOIN LATERAL` | No (inner) | Only customers with ≥1 order | | `LEFT JOIN LATERAL … ON true` | Yes | Include customers with empty result (NULLs) | | Plain `JOIN` | N/A | Cannot reference outer row | | Correlated `IN (SELECT …)` | Depends | Single column only | > **Tip:** Index matters: `CREATE INDEX ON orders(customer_id, order_date DESC, id)` lets each LATERAL subquery do an Index Scan returning 3 rows — no sort. For 10K customers that’s 10K tiny index scans vs one giant window sort. ```sql -- Top 3 most recent orders per customer (keeps customers with no orders) SELECT c.id, c.name, o.id AS order_id, o.total, o.created_at FROM customers c LEFT JOIN LATERAL ( SELECT id, total, created_at FROM orders WHERE customer_id = c.id ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 3 ) o ON true ORDER BY c.id, o.created_at DESC; -- CROSS JOIN LATERAL variant (only customers with orders) -- Replace LEFT JOIN LATERAL … ON true with CROSS JOIN LATERAL (...) -- With extra filter inside LATERAL (only completed orders) -- WHERE customer_id = c.id AND status = 'completed' ```

title: LATERAL vs Window Function vs Correlated Subquery for top-N per group — which scales when?
description: Compare execution strategies, index requirements, and planner choices for grouped top-N queries at scale.
answer:
Small number of groups + selective index → `LATERAL` wins (N index scans). Many groups or no supporting index → `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY)` single scan+sort wins. Correlated `IN` is limited to one column and rarely optimal.
| Approach | Best when | Index needed | Scales to | |---|---|---|---| | `LATERAL LIMIT N` | Few outer rows (≤100K), high selectivity | `(group_id, sort_key)` | 10K groups × 3 rows = fast | | `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY …)` | Many groups, or no per-group index | Single sort or `group_id, sort_key` index | Millions of groups, one pass | | Correlated `WHERE id = (SELECT max …)` | Single column, one per group | Similar to LATERAL | Limited; planner may flatten | | `DISTINCT ON` (PG) | Need one row per group (N=1) | `(group_id, sort_key)` | Fast PG-specific shortcut | > **Tip:** Check `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`: LATERAL shows `Nested Loop` with `Index Scan` per outer row (`loops=10000`). Window shows `WindowAgg` + `Sort`. If LATERAL loops count is huge (1M), the window will likely be faster — let the planner decide and test with real data size. ```sql -- Window alternative for same “top 3 per customer” WITH ranked AS ( SELECT c.id AS customer_id, o.id, o.total, o.created_at, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY o.customer_id ORDER BY o.created_at DESC) AS rn FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id ) SELECT * FROM ranked WHERE rn <= 3 ORDER BY customer_id, created_at DESC; -- Postgres DISTINCT ON for N=1 (fastest for “latest per group”) SELECT DISTINCT ON (customer_id) customer_id, id, total, created_at FROM orders ORDER BY customer_id, created_at DESC; ```

title: pgvector cosine similarity index in 2025-26 — HNSW vs IVFFlat for semantic search at scale?
description: Build a cosine-distance ANN index for embeddings, normalize vectors, and tune HNSW parameters.
answer:
Use `vector_cosine_ops` with **HNSW** in 2025-26 — faster builds, incremental inserts, better recall. Normalize vectors on write so `<=>` equals true cosine distance; set `m`, `ef_construction`, and query-time `ef_search` / `hnsw.ef_search`.
| Index | Build | Recall/latency | Needs training | Incremental inserts | |---|---|---|---|---| | `HNSW` (PG 16+, pgvector 0.7+) | Fast, no training | High recall, low latency | No | Yes (graph inserts) | | `IVFFlat` | Slow, needs `lists` tuning | Lower recall, needs `probes` | Yes (`lists*1000` rows) | No (rebuild) | | `IVFFlat` `lists` | `rows / 1000` heuristic | More lists = higher recall, slower | — | — | | Distance ops | `<=>` cosine, `<->` L2, `<#>` inner product | Pick `vector_cosine_ops` etc. | — | — | > **Tip:** For cosine you *must* normalize: `UPDATE docs SET embedding = embedding / ||embedding||` or normalize in app (`vec / np.linalg.norm(vec)`). Create index *after* bulk load for IVFFlat; HNSW tolerates incremental builds. Monitor `EXPLAIN` for `Index Scan using hnsw`. ```sql -- 1. Enable extension & store normalized 1536-dim embeddings CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector; CREATE TABLE docs ( id bigserial PRIMARY KEY, content text, embedding vector(1536) ); -- Normalize on insert (app side or trigger) -- INSERT INTO docs(content, embedding) VALUES ($1, $2::vector / ($2::vector <#> 0)) -- 2. HNSW cosine index (recommended 2025+) CREATE INDEX docs_embedding_hnsw_idx ON docs USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops) WITH (m = 16, ef_construction = 64); -- 3. Query: cosine distance (0 = identical, 2 = opposite) SET hnsw.ef_search = 100; -- higher = better recall, slower SELECT id, content, embedding <=> $1::vector AS distance FROM docs ORDER BY embedding <=> $1::vector LIMIT 10; -- Legacy IVFFlat (only if on older PG) -- CREATE INDEX ON docs USING ivfflat (embedding vector_cosine_ops) WITH (lists = 100); ```

title: Filtered vector search with pgvector — how do you combine WHERE category = 'X' with ORDER BY embedding <=> $1?
description: Solve pre-filter vs post-filter ANN problem using partial indexes or iterative scan for correct recall.
answer:
Naïve `WHERE … ORDER BY vec <=> $1 LIMIT` post-filters and may return < LIMIT rows. Fix with a **partial HNSW index** per hot filter, or enable **iterative scan** (pgvector 0.6+) so the executor keeps scanning until LIMIT is satisfied after filtering.
| Strategy | Recall | When to use | |---|---|---| | Naïve post-filter | Broken (may miss rows) | Never for filtered ANN | | Partial index `WHERE category='books'` | Perfect, fast | Few distinct filter values, high volume per value | | Iterative scan (`SET hnsw.iterative_scan`) | Correct, good perf | Ad-hoc filters, many combinations | | Pre-filter + brute force | Perfect, slow | Small filtered subset (<10K rows) | | Hybrid (partitioned tables) | High | Category cardinality very high | > **Tip:** For pgvector ≥0.6: `SET hnsw.iterative_scan = 'relaxed_order'` (or `strict_order` for exact ordering) — then a plain `WHERE category='X' ORDER BY vec <=> $1 LIMIT 10` works correctly. Always `EXPLAIN` to confirm `Hnsw Scan` with filter, not `Seq Scan`. ```sql -- Option A: partial HNSW per category (best when 5-20 hot categories) CREATE INDEX docs_books_hnsw ON docs USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops) WHERE category = 'books'; CREATE INDEX docs_electronics_hnsw ON docs USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops) WHERE category = 'electronics'; SELECT id, embedding <=> $1::vector AS dist FROM docs WHERE category = 'books' ORDER BY embedding <=> $1::vector LIMIT 10; -- Option B: single index + iterative scan (flexible, 2025+) SET hnsw.ef_search = 100; -- pgvector 0.7+: server handles iterative scan automatically when WHERE + ORDER BY vec present SELECT id, embedding <=> $1::vector AS dist FROM docs WHERE category = 'books' AND price < 100 ORDER BY embedding <=> $1::vector LIMIT 10; -- Fallback brute force for tiny filtered sets SELECT id FROM docs WHERE category = 'rare' ORDER BY embedding <=> $1 LIMIT 10; -- seq scan OK if <10K rows ```

title: How do you read EXPLAIN ANALYZE — cost, actual time, rows, and Buffers?
description: Decode execution plans, spot cardinality misestimates, and use BUFFERS/SETTINGS to debug I/O.
answer:
`EXPLAIN` shows estimates; `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` actually runs and shows `actual time`, `rows`, `loops`, and `Buffers: shared hit/read`. A 10× gap between estimated and actual rows means stale stats — run `ANALYZE`.
| Field | Meaning | Red flag | |---|---|---| | `cost=0.00..123.45` | Estimated startup..total cost (arbitrary units) | Huge cost on seq scan → missing index | | `rows=1000` (estimate) | Planner’s expected rows | Off by 10× → bad `n_distinct` / stats | | `actual time=0.1..12.3 rows=50 loops=100` | Real time per loop & actual rows | `loops` multiplies cost for nested loops | | `Buffers: shared hit=10 read=200` | Pages hit in cache vs read from disk | High `read` → cold cache / large table | | `Planning Time / Execution Time` | Parse vs run | High planning → many partitions / complex query | > **Tip:** Run `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, VERBOSE)` on a **replica** or `BEGIN; EXPLAIN ANALYZE …; ROLLBACK;` for writes. Use `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, FORMAT JSON)` with `https://explain.depesz.com` or `pev2` visualizers for big plans. ```sql -- Basic EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42; -- Gold standard (actually executes; beware large writes) EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, VERBOSE) SELECT c.name, COUNT(o.id) FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE c.country = 'US' GROUP BY c.name; -- Check stats health when estimates are off SELECT relname, last_analyze, last_autoanalyze, n_live_tup FROM pg_stat_all_tables WHERE relname = 'orders'; -- Fix: ANALYZE orders; -- or increase stats target ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN customer_id SET STATISTICS 500; ```

title: EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows Seq Scan on a 10M-row table — how do you diagnose and fix it?
description: Trace sequential scans to missing indexes, function-wrapped columns, or stale statistics and verify the fix.
answer:
A `Seq Scan` on a large table in `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` means no usable index or the planner thinks seq is cheaper. Check: 1) index exists, 2) `WHERE` matches index (no `LOWER(col)`), 3) selectivity, 4) stats freshness (`ANALYZE`), 5) parameter sniffing.
| Cause | Symptom in plan | Fix | |---|---|---| | No index | `Seq Scan on orders` `Filter: customer_id=…` | `CREATE INDEX ON orders(customer_id)` | | Function on column | `Filter: lower(email)=…` never uses `email` index | Expression index `ON lower(email)` | | Low selectivity (30% rows) | Planner correctly picks Seq Scan | Keep seq; or use `Bitmap Heap Scan` range | | Stale stats | `rows est 10` vs `actual 50000` | `ANALYZE` + higher `STATISTICS` target | | Wrong type / collation mismatch | `Filter` not `Index Cond` | Align types (`text` vs `varchar`, `uuid`) | > **Tip:** After creating an index, re-run `ANALYZE table;` then `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` — look for `Index Scan` or `Bitmap Heap Scan` and `Buffers: shared hit` dropping dramatically. Use `pg_stat_user_indexes` to verify the index is actually hit in prod. ```sql -- Diagnose: is the Seq Scan justified? EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42; -- Seq Scan on orders (cost=0.00..180000 rows=1 width=100) (actual rows=12000 loops=1) -- Filter: (customer_id = 42) -- ← should be Index Cond, not Filter! -- Buffers: shared read=15000 -- high read = no index -- Fix 1: create index + analyze CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_customer_id ON orders(customer_id); ANALYZE orders; -- Fix 2: expression index for function-wrapped column CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_users_lower_email ON users (lower(email)); -- Now: WHERE lower(email) = lower('A@B.com') uses Index Scan -- Fix 3: verify index is used EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42; -- Index Scan using idx_orders_customer_id … Buffers: shared hit=45 ✓ ```

title: Seq Scan vs Index Scan vs Index-Only Scan — when does Postgres choose each?
description: Explain planner cost model, visibility map, and covering indexes for read-heavy workloads.
answer:
The planner estimates cost from `seq_page_cost` vs `random_page_cost` × selectivity. Highly selective (`<5%` rows) → `Index Scan`; moderately selective → `Bitmap Heap Scan`; all columns in index + `VACUUM` clean → `Index-Only Scan`; otherwise → `Seq Scan`.
| Scan type | Reads | When chosen | Requirement | |---|---|---|---| | `Seq Scan` | All heap pages sequentially | >5-10% rows, small table, or no index | None | | `Index Scan` | Index + random heap fetches | <5% rows, selective filter | Index on filter cols | | `Bitmap Heap Scan` | Bitmap → sorted heap reads | 5-30% rows, multiple indexes | Indexes to bitmap-AND/OR | | `Index-Only Scan` | Index pages only | Query columns ⊆ index & VM clean | `INCLUDE` cols + `VACUUM` | > **Tip:** Make an `Index-Only Scan` possible with `CREATE INDEX ON orders(customer_id) INCLUDE (total, status)` and regular `VACUUM` (sets visibility map). Check `EXPLAIN` for `Heap Fetches: 0` — if high, run `VACUUM` or increase `autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor`. ```sql -- Covering index for: SELECT total, status FROM orders WHERE customer_id = $1 CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_cust_cover ON orders (customer_id) INCLUDE (total, status); VACUUM ANALYZE orders; -- sets visibility map for index-only EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT total, status FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42; -- Index Only Scan using idx_orders_cust_cover (Heap Fetches: 0) ✓ -- Buffers: shared hit=4 (vs 15000 for seq scan) -- Bitmap example for OR / multi-index EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42 OR status = 'pending'; -- BitmapOr -> Bitmap Heap Scan (combines two indexes) ```

title: Covering indexes (INCLUDE) and Bitmap Heap Scans — how do you eliminate heap fetches in 2025?
description: Design INCLUDE indexes for index-only scans and understand when bitmap scans batch random I/O.
answer:
`INCLUDE (col)` adds non-key payload to an index for `Index-Only Scans` without bloating the B-tree. `Bitmap Heap Scan` batches index lookups into sorted TIDs for sequential-ish heap reads — ideal for medium selectivity or `OR` queries.
| Pattern | Index | Benefit | |---|---|---| | Covering for filtered select | `ON t(a) INCLUDE (b,c)` | No heap fetch if VM clean | | Composite for range + sort | `ON t(a, b DESC)` | Filter + `ORDER BY` without sort | | Expression covering | `ON lower(email) INCLUDE (id)` | Case-insensitive lookup, index-only | | Multi-index OR | Two indexes → `BitmapOr` | Efficient `WHERE a=1 OR b=2` without seq scan | > **Tip:** `INCLUDE` columns don’t help with `WHERE` or `ORDER BY` — they’re payload only. Keep `autovacuum` aggressive (`autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor=0.05` for hot tables) so the visibility map stays fresh and `Heap Fetches` stays near zero. ```sql -- Before: Index Scan with heap fetches (random I/O) CREATE INDEX ON orders(customer_id); EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT id, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42; -- Index Scan … Heap Fetches: 120 (random reads) -- After: Index-Only Scan (no heap) DROP INDEX idx1; CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_cover ON orders(customer_id) INCLUDE (total); VACUUM ANALYZE orders; EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42; -- total is covered -- Index Only Scan … Heap Fetches: 0 ✓ -- Bitmap Heap Scan for medium selectivity EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) SELECT * FROM events WHERE user_id = 42 OR session_id = 'abc'; -- BitmapOr -> Bitmap Heap Scan (rows=5000, well above index-scan threshold) ```

title: Transaction isolation levels in Postgres — what anomalies does each level prevent?
description: Map Read Committed / Repeatable Read / Serializable to dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, and phantoms.
answer:
Postgres has 3 levels (Read Uncommitted ≡ Read Committed). `READ COMMITTED` = per-statement snapshot. `REPEATABLE READ` = txn snapshot, no non-repeatable reads. `SERIALIZABLE` (SSI) = no phantoms/write-skew but aborts on serialization failures — retry required.
| Level (PG) | Dirty read | Non-repeatable read | Phantom | Implementation | |---|---|---|---|---| | Read Committed (default) | ✗ | allowed | allowed | New snapshot each statement | | Repeatable Read | ✗ | ✗ | ✗* (*PG snapshot prevents) | Snapshot at txn start | | Serializable (SSI) | ✗ | ✗ | ✗ (detected) | SSI + 40001 abort | | Read Uncommitted | ✗ (same as RC in PG) | — | — | PG maps to RC | > **Tip:** Default `READ COMMITTED` + `SELECT … FOR UPDATE` often beats `SERIALIZABLE` for explicit row locking. Reserve `SERIALIZABLE` for true invariant checks (e.g., no overlapping bookings) where a `FOR UPDATE` predicate is hard to express. ```sql -- Default: each statement sees latest committed data BEGIN; -- READ COMMITTED (default) SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id=1; -- sees committed value -- concurrent txn commits new balance here SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id=1; -- may see different value (non-repeatable) COMMIT; -- Repeatable Read: snapshot frozen at first query BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ; SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id=1; -- snapshot -- concurrent commit invisible until this txn ends SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id=1; -- same as before COMMIT; -- Serializable: detects anomalies, throws 40001 BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE; -- ... invariant checks ... COMMIT; -- may error: could not serialize access due to concurrent update ```

title: Serializable isolation pitfalls — write skew, retry storms, and when advisory locks beat SSI?
description: Handle 40001 serialization failures with idempotent retries and choose pessimistic locking for hot spots.
answer:
`SERIALIZABLE` (SSI) prevents write-skew by aborting one of two concurrent txns that together violate an invariant (`ERROR 40001`). The app *must* retry the whole txn with backoff. For hot rows, `FOR UPDATE` or `pg_advisory_xact_lock` is faster than retry storms.
| Approach | Latency | Throughput under contention | Complexity | |---|---|---|---| | `SERIALIZABLE` | Higher (abort+retry) | Drops sharply at >10% write contention | Retry loop, idempotency | | `SELECT … FOR UPDATE` | Blocks, no retry | Better for single-row invariants | Must lock correct rows | | `pg_advisory_xact_lock(key)` | Blocks on app key | Best for multi-row / cross-table invariants | Manual key hashing | | Optimistic `WHERE version = $old` | Low when no conflict | Good for low contention | Version column | > **Tip:** Wrap serializable txns in an idempotent retry helper with jitter: `for i in 1..3: try txn; except 40001: sleep(rand*2^i)`. Ensure the txn body is side-effect free until `COMMIT` (no external HTTP calls inside!). ```sql -- Write-skew prone: two concurrent txns each check “at least one doctor on call” BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE; SELECT COUNT(*) FROM doctors WHERE on_call = true; -- both see 1 -- each txn sets a different doctor to off_call, expecting 1 remains UPDATE doctors SET on_call = false WHERE id = $1; -- one txn will be aborted at COMMIT with 40001 COMMIT; -- Alternative: pessimistic advisory lock (no retry storm) BEGIN; SELECT pg_advisory_xact_lock(42); -- 42 = on_call invariant key (hash) UPDATE doctors SET on_call = false WHERE id = $1 AND on_call = true; -- check invariant while holding lock SELECT COUNT(*) FROM doctors WHERE on_call = true; -- always correct COMMIT; -- lock released -- App retry pseudocode -- for attempt in 1..3: -- try: run_serializable_txn(); break -- except SerializationFailure: sleep(random()*2**attempt) ```

title: SKIP LOCKED for job queues — how do you build a concurrent queue without race conditions?
description: Use FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED with a CTE UPDATE … RETURNING to atomically claim jobs for many workers.
answer:
`SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 1` skips rows locked by other workers instead of blocking. Combine with a CTE that `UPDATE status='processing' RETURNING *` to claim atomically — no double-processing, no polling races.
| Pattern | Query | Workers scale | |---|---|---| | Naïve `SELECT then UPDATE` | Race: two workers pick same row | Broken at ≥2 workers | | `FOR UPDATE` (blocking) | Second worker waits | Serial, not concurrent | | `FOR UPDATE NOWAIT` | Second worker errors | Needs catch & retry | | `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` | Second worker skips to next free row | Linear scale to many workers | > **Tip:** Always `ORDER BY priority DESC, id` inside the CTE so workers claim highest priority first and ordering is deterministic. Add `WHERE status='pending' AND run_at <= now()` and index `ON jobs(status, run_at, priority)` for fast claims. ```sql -- Atomic claim: pick 1 pending job, mark processing, return it WITH claimed AS ( SELECT id FROM jobs WHERE status = 'pending' AND run_at <= now() ORDER BY priority DESC, id FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 1 ) UPDATE jobs j SET status = 'processing', claimed_at = now(), claimed_by = $1 FROM claimed c WHERE j.id = c.id RETURNING j.*; -- Index for fast claim (partial index keeps it small) CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_jobs_claim ON jobs (priority DESC, id) WHERE status = 'pending'; -- Worker loop (pseudo): -- loop: job = run_above(); if !job sleep 500ms; else process(job) ```

title: FOR UPDATE vs FOR UPDATE NOWAIT vs FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED — which to use when?
description: Compare row-level locking modes for queues, user-facing “busy” signals, and batch processors.

title: UPSERT with INSERT … ON CONFLICT — how do you insert or update atomically without races?
description: Use ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE vs DO NOTHING, the EXCLUDED pseudo-table, and required unique constraints.
answer:
`INSERT … ON CONFLICT (unique_col) DO UPDATE SET col = EXCLUDED.col` is an atomic upsert. It requires a `UNIQUE`/`PRIMARY KEY` constraint on the conflict target. `EXCLUDED` refers to the row that *would* have been inserted.
| Variant | Behavior | Needs | |---|---|---| | `ON CONFLICT (email) DO UPDATE` | Insert or overwrite | `UNIQUE(email)` | | `ON CONFLICT (email) DO NOTHING` | Insert or ignore | `UNIQUE(email)` — idempotent ingest | | `ON CONFLICT ON CONSTRAINT name` | Named constraint target | Explicit constraint name (supports composite) | | `MERGE` (PG 15+) | SQL-standard upsert with richer conditions | PG 15+ | > **Tip:** For partial upserts (soft-delete), use a partial unique index: `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON users(email) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL` then `ON CONFLICT (email) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL DO UPDATE …`. Without the `WHERE` clause the conflict target won’t match. ```sql -- Basic upsert: insert or update name INSERT INTO users (email, name, updated_at) VALUES ('a@b.com', 'Alice', now()) ON CONFLICT (email) DO UPDATE SET name = EXCLUDED.name, updated_at = EXCLUDED.updated_at RETURNING id, xmax = 0 AS inserted; -- xmax trick: true if inserted -- Idempotent ingest (ignore duplicates) INSERT INTO events (id, payload) VALUES (123, '{"x":1}') ON CONFLICT (id) DO NOTHING RETURNING id; -- returns 0 rows if conflicted -- Composite key upsert INSERT INTO stats (user_id, day, count) VALUES (42, '2025-08-26', 1) ON CONFLICT (user_id, day) DO UPDATE SET count = stats.count + 1; -- MERGE (PG 15+, SQL standard, supports DELETE branch) MERGE INTO users u USING (VALUES ('a@b.com','Alice')) AS v(email,name) ON u.email = v.email WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET name = v.name WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (email,name) VALUES (v.email, v.name); ```

title: Advanced UPSERT patterns — conditional updates, xmax detection, and soft-delete-aware indexes?
description: Build idempotent pipelines with WHERE on DO UPDATE, RETURNING to detect insert vs update, and partial indexes.
answer:
Add `DO UPDATE … WHERE EXCLUDED.updated_at > users.updated_at` to keep newest-wins, use `RETURNING (xmax=0)` to tell insert from update, and match conflict targets to **partial unique indexes** for soft-delete tables.
| Pattern | SQL snippet | Why | |---|---|---| | Newest-wins | `DO UPDATE SET … WHERE EXCLUDED.ts > t.ts` | Prevent stale overwrite from out-of-order events | | Detect insert vs update | `RETURNING *, (xmax=0) AS inserted` | Branch logic (e.g., send welcome only on insert) | | Soft-delete aware | `ON CONFLICT (email) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL` | Allow re-insert after soft delete | | Counter increment | `DO UPDATE SET count = t.count + EXCLUDED.count` | Idempotent aggregation | > **Tip:** `xmax = 0` is an undocumented-but-stable trick: freshly inserted rows have `xmax=0`, updated rows get a new `xmax`. For a documented alternative, use a CTE: `WITH ins AS (INSERT … ON CONFLICT … DO UPDATE … RETURNING *) SELECT …` and compare `created_at`. ```sql -- Newest-wins upsert (ignore stale events) INSERT INTO profiles (user_id, name, updated_at) VALUES (42, 'Alice', '2025-08-26 10:00') ON CONFLICT (user_id) DO UPDATE SET name = EXCLUDED.name, updated_at = EXCLUDED.updated_at WHERE EXCLUDED.updated_at > profiles.updated_at; -- only if newer -- Detect inserted vs updated (xmax trick) WITH upsert AS ( INSERT INTO users (email, name) VALUES ('a@b.com','Alice') ON CONFLICT (email) DO UPDATE SET name = EXCLUDED.name RETURNING *, (xmax = 0) AS was_inserted ) SELECT *, CASE WHEN was_inserted THEN 'welcome email' ELSE 'no email' END FROM upsert; -- Soft-delete aware CREATE UNIQUE INDEX uniq_users_email_active ON users(email) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL; INSERT INTO users (email, name) VALUES ('a@b.com','Alice') ON CONFLICT (email) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL DO UPDATE SET name = EXCLUDED.name; ```

title: JSONB querying and GIN indexing — how do you query and index schemaless data efficiently?
description: Use @>, ->, ->>, ?, and GIN with jsonb_path_ops vs default ops for containment vs path extraction.
answer:
Store as `JSONB` (binary, indexable). Use `@>` for containment (“contains this JSON”), `->`/`->>` for path extraction, and `?` for key existence. Index with `GIN` — `jsonb_path_ops` is smaller/faster for `@>` only; default `jsonb_ops` supports `@>`, `?`, `?&`.
| Operator | Example | Uses GIN? | Note | |---|---|---|---| | `@>` contains | `data @> '{"role":"admin"}'` | Yes (both GIN types) | Most important for filtering | | `->` `->>` | `data->'address'->>'city' = 'NYC'` | No (needs expression BTREE) | Use expression index for this pattern | | `?` exists | `data ? 'email'` | Yes (default `jsonb_ops` only) | `jsonb_path_ops` does NOT support `?` | | `@?` JSONPath | `data @? '$.tags[*] ? (@ == "vip")'` | Yes (PG 12+) | Rich queries, GIN-accelerated | > **Tip:** For “query one hot field” (e.g., `data->>'email'`), a BTREE expression index `CREATE INDEX ON users ((data->>'email'))` beats a GIN — it supports `=`/`ORDER BY`. Reserve GIN for ad-hoc containment searches over many keys. ```sql -- Table with JSONB CREATE TABLE users (id bigserial PRIMARY KEY, data jsonb); INSERT INTO users(data) VALUES ('{"name":"Alice","tags":["vip","beta"],"addr":{"city":"NYC"}}'), ('{"name":"Bob","role":"admin","addr":{"city":"SF"}}'); -- Containment (GIN-friendly) SELECT * FROM users WHERE data @> '{"role":"admin"}'; SELECT * FROM users WHERE data @> '{"addr":{"city":"NYC"}}'; -- Key existence & JSONPath SELECT * FROM users WHERE data ? 'role'; SELECT * FROM users WHERE data @? '$.tags[*] ? (@ == "vip")'; -- Indexes CREATE INDEX idx_users_gin ON users USING gin (data); -- default jsonb_ops (versatile) -- CREATE INDEX idx_users_gin_path ON users USING gin (data jsonb_path_ops); -- smaller, @> only CREATE INDEX idx_users_email ON users ((data->>'email')); -- for WHERE data->>'email' = 'a@b.com' -- Query with expression index SELECT * FROM users WHERE data->>'email' = 'alice@example.com'; -- uses idx_users_email ```

title: JSONB vs normalized columns vs EAV — how do you model flexible attributes without killing query performance?
description: Choose between pure JSONB, hybrid (hot columns + JSONB), and normalized/EAV based on query patterns and schema volatility.
answer:
Pure `JSONB` is flexible but slower for joins/filters; normalized columns are fastest for hot, query-heavy fields. The **hybrid** model — hot fields as real columns + cold/sparse fields in `JSONB` — wins for most evolving apps. Use `EAV` only for extreme sparsity with typed values.
| Model | Query speed (hot field) | Flexibility | Indexing | Joins/FKs | |---|---|---|---|---| | Pure JSONB | Slow (GIN or expression index) | Highest — schemaless | GIN + expression | No FK on attrs | | Hybrid ⭐ | Fast (BTREE) + flexible tail | High — add real cols as needed | BTREE (hot) + GIN (cold) | FKs on hot cols | | Normalized (separate table) | Fastest (indexed cols) | Low — migration per attr | BTREE everywhere | Full FK, joins | | EAV (row per attr) | Slow (pivot / self-joins) | Very high | Hard (generic) | Type safety tricky | > **Tip:** Start hybrid: promote any JSONB field that gets filtered/joined/sorted to a real column with a BTREE index. Add a `CHECK` to keep them in sync or use a generated column: `email text GENERATED ALWAYS AS (data->>'email') STORED`. ```sql -- Hybrid model: hot fields are columns, flex attrs in JSONB CREATE TABLE products ( id bigserial PRIMARY KEY, sku text UNIQUE NOT NULL, price numeric NOT NULL, -- hot: BTREE, FK, range queries category text NOT NULL, -- hot: BTREE attrs jsonb DEFAULT '{}', -- cold/sparse: GIN email text GENERATED ALWAYS AS (attrs->>'email') STORED -- sync example ); CREATE INDEX ON products(category); CREATE INDEX ON products USING gin (attrs); CREATE INDEX ON products ((attrs->>'color')) WHERE attrs ? 'color'; -- Fast hybrid queries SELECT * FROM products WHERE category = 'shoes' AND price < 100; -- BTREE SELECT * FROM products WHERE attrs @> '{"color":"red"}'; -- GIN SELECT * FROM products WHERE attrs->>'size' = 'M'; -- expression index -- Promote hot attr to column when it becomes query-heavy: -- ALTER TABLE products ADD COLUMN color text GENERATED ALWAYS AS (attrs->>'color') STORED; -- CREATE INDEX ON products(color); ```
